\title{Does a tyre-degradation model transfer?\\
\large Cross-championship evidence and a retrospective audit of
\NDecisions{} real pit-stop decisions}

\author{Mohammed Reda Medjadj \\ Independent}

\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\linenumbers

\begin{abstract}
Race-strategy models are usually fitted and validated inside one championship.
Does a fitted model predict a season it
has never seen, and does its recommendation resemble what a team did? I apply one protocol to both across \NClasses{} car classes and
four championships --- Formula~1, WEC, IMSA and ELMS --- common rather than
identical, since endurance sources carry no tyre compound.

Four findings. Degradation slopes transfer as a property of the
\emph{circuit-class}, not the championship, and rarely: of \NCircuitClasses{}
measured by leave-one-race-out, \NTransferAboveTwo{} reach a within-stint $R^2$
of $\TransferThreshold{}$. That count overstates instability. With a slope
stable by construction, \NCeilingBelowThreshold{} of \NCeilingCircuits{}
Formula~1 circuits cannot clear the threshold against their own lap noise;
pricing it in leaves \NCeilingUnstable{} unstable and \NCeilingStable{} stable.
Neither real Pirelli compounds nor Friday long runs improve it.
Whether an extra stop pays is set by its cost: over \NRaceSeasons{}
race-seasons, pit loss alone separates the regimes at an AUC of
\RegimeAucPitLoss{} against \RegimeAucSlope{} for degradation. Replaying
\NDecisions{} real first stops with each team's own next stop held fixed, a
time-optimal planner lands a median of \CommitAllAfter{} laps from the team in
Formula~1 and no endurance gap is established; \CommitOneAfter{} remains in
one-stop races, worth tenths of a second a lap. Run to the flag instead, the same planner is \FoneMedian{}
late: it must be asked the pit wall's question.
And the rival such a model should answer is under-determined:
\NRivalRules{} defensible rules agree on \NRivalAllAgree{} of
\NRivalAllApply{} decisions.
\end{abstract}

\vspace{0.6em}
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} race strategy; tyre degradation; out-of-sample
validation; motorsport analytics; Formula~1; endurance racing; pit stop
optimisation; retrospective audit

\doublespacing

\section{Introduction}

A pit stop is a decision under uncertainty with a measurable cost. The
literature on optimising it is small but real, and this paper's contribution is
not another optimiser. It is a pair of validation questions that the existing
work, for understandable reasons, does not ask.

The first is \emph{transfer}. A degradation model is fitted on races that have
happened and used on a race that has not. Whether a slope fitted on past seasons
of a circuit predicts the next season of that circuit is an empirical question,
and answering it requires holding a season out --- which in turn requires more
than one season, and ideally more than one championship.

The second is \emph{agreement with practice}. A model that recommends a stop lap
can be compared to the lap a team actually chose. This is not a claim about
which was faster; it is a measurement of where a model and a professional pit
wall part company, and by how much.

Both questions need breadth to answer, and breadth is what this work supplies:
one protocol, four championships, \NClasses{} car classes, every quantity
measured from published timing or absent.

The protocol is the object of this paper and the findings are what it
returned. Two of them came back negative, which is a property of the answers
rather than of the apparatus. The cost falls in the other direction: my
modelling is simpler than much of the work I cite, I ignore energy management
entirely, and nothing here makes an existing optimiser better.

\section{Related work}

Race-strategy research is largely about building the optimiser. The methods vary
widely --- discrete-event simulation, Monte Carlo, dynamic programming,
mixed-integer programming, reinforcement learning, game theory --- and the goal
is consistent: compute a better plan than a team would otherwise choose.

\citet{bekker2009} give the earliest sustained operations-research treatment,
simulating a full race with overtaking and traffic under the refuelling rules of
the time. \citet{heilmeier2018} introduce the lap-time decomposition that much of
the later work rests on, combining fuel mass, tyre degradation and driver
effects, and \citet{heilmeier2020mc} extend it to a probabilistic simulation
sampling accidents, safety cars and lap-time variability. \citet{heilmeier2020nn}
then train neural networks on that simulation's output to make calls in real
time. \citet{carrasco2022} give an exact dynamic program over stop laps and
compound choice, extended to a stochastic version, and \citet{aguad2024}
formulate the problem as a zero-sum feedback Stackelberg game between two
drivers, finding that a strategic competitor gains over 15\% in winning odds.
Outside Formula~1 the same machinery has been built for endurance racing, and
almost entirely for electric cars, where the binding constraint is charge rather
than fuel. \citet{vankampen2022} solve endurance stint planning and powertrain
operation jointly under thermal limits; \citet{vankampen2024} extend that to
model predictive control that prices a competitor's likely response; and
\citet{devries2026} pose the whole problem as a two-agent game, solving a
game-theoretic optimal control problem per lap and training reinforcement
learning agents to allocate energy and schedule stops over a race.
\citet{boettinger2023} is the rare treatment of GT racing rather than
single-seaters, simulating the Nordschleife and learning a stop policy from fuel
mass and race position. Recent Formula~1 work adds learning: \citet{thomas2025}
apply explainable reinforcement learning to compound and stop timing,
\citet{fieni2025} combine a mixed-integer program with an RL agent over energy,
tyre wear and pit timing, \citet{fieni2026} extend that to self-play among
competing agents, and \citet{todd2025} forecast tyre energy from team-internal
telemetry. \citet{santillana2026}
deploys a calibrated real-time Monte Carlo engine live, generating
natural-language briefings faithful to its own probabilistic state.

Two things are rare across all of it.

The first is out-of-sample validation of the fitted parameters. A tyre model is
fitted and its quality reported on the data it was fitted to. \citet{cappello2026}
come closest, building a Bayesian state-space model of degradation from the same
public timing source used here, with lap time as fuel mass plus a latent tyre
state and pit stops as resets. They also validate out of sample, and are the
only work here that does: \citet{cappello2026} evaluate predictive robustness
on 19 race sessions of the 2025 season, by rolling-origin
cross-validation against an AR(1) benchmark. What separates that from this
paper is the axis along which the held-out data varies. Their held-out sessions
are one season, one driver and one
championship, held out forward in time; the protocol here holds out a whole
season of a circuit-class and asks whether the remaining seasons predict it,
over \NCircuitClasses{} circuit-classes and four championships. Both are
out-of-sample. Only one changes season, circuit and class at once. They also
report compound-specific degradation differences as not statistically distinct.
That is consistent with the instability I measure at scale.

The second is comparison against what teams actually did. Optimisers get
compared to other optimisers, to author-constructed baselines, or to the optimum
under the model's own assumptions. \citet{bekker2009} compare to real races, and
\citet{aguad2024} compare strategic against non-strategic agents inside their
own game, but I am not aware of work that replays a large sample of real
pit-stop decisions and reports where the optimiser and the pit wall diverge.

A third gap is narrower and sits between the two. A model's assumptions can be
tested against measured parameter values without testing the model itself.
\citet{salminen2026} solves the two-car one-stop game analytically and derives
the earliest lap on which an undercut cannot be answered, which is the only
mechanism I have found that predicts stopping \emph{before} the time optimum
--- the direction of my third result. His overcut defence requires a tyre
advantage of $(o + \varepsilon)/\theta$ laps. At the degradation rates fitted
here it is unreachable on a substantial share of circuit-compounds, which I
report in the repository because it tests a model that is not mine. His
position-keeping defence is a different matter: it is the third candidate
explanation for my own Result~3, so I implement it, test it on the same
\NDecisionsFone{} Formula~1 decisions, and report in
Section~\ref{sec:thirdexplanation} that it fails.

The modelling here is not more sophisticated than \citet{heilmeier2020mc} or
\citet{aguad2024}; in places it is deliberately simpler, and it ignores energy
management entirely.
What is different is the protocol: of the \NCatalogued{} papers catalogued for
this review, \citet{cappello2026} is the only one that validates its fitted
parameters on data it did not fit, and none applies a single protocol to more
than one championship. I claim no priority. The literature is large and a
catalogue is not a census; the claim is only that these
\NCatalogued{} papers, each checked against a publication record, do not
contain the comparison this paper reports. Two of the four findings that come
back from it are negative.

\section{Data and protocol}

\subsection{Sources and scope}

Formula~1 lap timing, tyre compound and per-lap track status come from the
FastF1 API. WEC, IMSA and ELMS timing comes from a community-maintained
endurance dataset carrying lap times, stint structure and flag state but
\emph{not} tyre compound. The endurance degradation models are therefore
net-slope models where the Formula~1 one is per compound, and that asymmetry is
restated wherever the two are compared. Two further Formula~1 sources serve
Section~\ref{sec:repairs} only: the compound Pirelli nominated for each race,
and second-practice laps from the OpenF1 API, which serves the same timing feed
from 2023 on. Table~\ref{tab:scope} gives the scope.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Scope. A race-season is one class at one circuit in one season, which
is the unit everything here is fitted and reported on.}
\label{tab:scope}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrl}
\toprule
& Classes & Circuits & Race-seasons & Replayed decisions & Seasons \\
\midrule
Formula~1 & 1 & \NCircuitsFone{} & \NRacesFone{} & \NDecisionsFone{} & \SeasonsFone{} \\
IMSA      & \NClassesImsa{} & \NCircuitsImsa{} & \NRacesImsa{} & \NDecisionsImsa{} & \SeasonsImsa{} \\
ELMS      & \NClassesElms{} & \NCircuitsElms{} & \NRacesElms{} & \NDecisionsElms{} & \SeasonsElms{} \\
WEC       & \NClassesWec{} & \NCircuitsWec{} & \NRacesWec{} & \NDecisionsWec{} & \SeasonsWec{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Nothing is imputed. Where a source lacks a quantity the affected layer is not
fitted, and the gap goes on the record as a gap.

\paragraph{Which laps are modelled.} Every fit here runs on a filtered frame
rather than on raw timing, and the filters matter enough to state. A lap enters
only if it is a green-flag racing lap: in-laps and out-laps are dropped, as are
laps under any neutralisation, laps the source marks inaccurate or deleted, and
laps whose time is missing. Wet-compound laps are excluded entirely, so every
degradation coefficient is a dry-weather quantity. What survives is then trimmed
against traffic, by dropping laps slower than a fixed multiple of that
driver--race's own median --- a relative threshold rather than an absolute one,
because the same gap in seconds means different things at Monaco and at Spa ---
and a stint is modelled only if enough laps survive the trim to fit a shape to.
The per-circuit counts at every stage are generated into the degradation
reports, so the cost of each filter is visible rather than asserted. What this
frame does \emph{not} remove is lap-level variation the filters cannot see: a
driver lifting to manage a tyre, an engine mode, a blue flag that cost less than
the trim threshold. The driver--race intercept absorbs a constant, not those.

\subsection{Degradation}

For driver--race $i$ and lap $\ell$ within stint $s$, with tyre age $a$ and
compound $c$,
%
\begin{equation}
y_{i\ell} \;=\; \alpha_i \;+\; \phi\,\ell \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{d}\beta_{c,k}\,a_{i\ell}^{\,k} \;+\; \varepsilon_{i\ell},
\label{eq:degradation}
\end{equation}
%
where $y$ is lap time, $\alpha_i$ is a driver--race fixed effect absorbing car
pace, driver pace and track conditions, and $\phi\ell$ is a fuel-burn proxy that
is identified only where refuelling is prohibited. In endurance, where cars
refuel, $\ell$ is replaced by laps since the last refuelling stop and the
compound index drops out, leaving a single net slope $\beta_1$.

Equation~\ref{eq:degradation} is estimated by ordinary least squares through
a Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse,
which handles the rank-deficient cases --- a driver--race seen on one compound
only. The polynomial degree $d \in \{1,2\}$ is chosen per circuit by
leave-one-race-out cross-validation.

Standard errors are cluster-robust (CR1) on the driver--race and referred to
$t(G-1)$ rather than the normal \citep{cameron2015}. The clustering is not
decorative: lap-to-lap errors within one driver's race are strongly dependent,
and a coverage simulation on synthetic races with realistic between-unit slope
variation puts the classical 95\% interval at roughly 75\% coverage against 95\%
for the robust one.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\textwidth]{s3_f1_degradation.png}
\caption{The fitted object itself: linear tyre-degradation coefficients for
Formula~1, by circuit and compound, with cluster-robust intervals.
\NCoefficientsFone{} coefficients across \NCircuitsFone{} circuits. Points
outside the plotted range are clipped and then named under the axis, because a
handful of extremes otherwise compresses every other circuit into a tenth of
the width.}
\label{fig:degradation}
\end{figure}

Two features of Figure~\ref{fig:degradation} constrain everything after it.
\NCoefCrossingZero{} of the
\NCoefficientsFone{} fitted slopes, \PctCoefCrossingZero{}\%, have a
cluster-robust interval containing zero: on those circuit--compound pairs I
cannot distinguish tyre degradation from none. And within a circuit,
\PctCompoundOverlap{}\% of compound pairs have overlapping intervals, so the
compound distinction the Formula~1 model carries is largely unresolved by the
data behind it. Both are reported, and neither is screened out: a slope that cannot be
distinguished from flat is still the measurement I have.
Section~\ref{sec:threats} returns to what this costs.

\subsection{Transfer}

Fit on every season of a circuit-class but one, predict the held-out season, and
score the within-stint demeaned residual:
%
\begin{equation}
R^{2}_{\text{within}} \;=\; 1 - \frac{\sum_{s}\sum_{\ell \in s}\bigl(\tilde{y}_{\ell} - \tilde{\hat{y}}_{\ell}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{s}\sum_{\ell \in s}\tilde{y}_{\ell}^{\,2}},
\qquad
\tilde{x}_{\ell} = x_{\ell} - \overline{x}_{s}.
\label{eq:transfer}
\end{equation}
%
The demeaning in Equation~\ref{eq:transfer} is what makes this a test of the
\emph{shape} of
degradation rather than of pace. A driver--race intercept fitted on training
data cannot be observed on a held-out race, so comparing raw lap times would
leak information through $\alpha_i$.

\subsection{The multi-stop dynamic program}

For an endurance race of $L$ laps with green pace $p$, net slope $\beta$, pit
loss $\pi$ and fuel range $F$, a plan is a partition of $L$ into stints
$(n_1,\dots,n_{m+1})$ with $m$ stops. Total time under the fitted model is
%
\begin{equation}
T(n_1,\dots,n_{m+1}) \;=\; m\pi \;+\; \sum_{j}\left(n_j p + \beta\,\frac{n_j(n_j+1)}{2}\right),
\label{eq:dp}
\end{equation}
%
subject to $n_j \le F$ for every stint. The triangular sum is the accumulated
tyre loss over a stint of $n_j$ laps. I use it exactly, not as the
$\beta n_j^{2}/2$ integral; they differ by $\beta n_j / 2$, which is about a
second over a forty-lap stint and is the only quantity the stop decision
compares against $\pi$.

Because $T$ in Equation~\ref{eq:dp} is separable across stints given $m$, the minimum over plans is a
one-dimensional dynamic program in remaining laps, solved exactly for each $m$
from the fuel minimum $\lceil L/F \rceil - 1$ upward. A race is called
\emph{tyre-limited} when the time-optimal $m$ exceeds that fuel minimum.

\subsection{The Monte Carlo engine and the decision audit}
\label{sec:method}

The single-next-stop engine evaluates every candidate pit lap over
\NDraws{} shared realisations. Each draw resamples the degradation and fuel
coefficients from their cluster-robust posteriors ($t(G-1)$ scaled by the
estimated standard errors), the neutralisation hazard from its Gamma posterior,
and lap noise at the cross-validated residual scale. Candidates share the same
draws, so a comparison between two pit laps carries no unrelated sampling
noise. Plans leaving fewer than \MinFinalStint{} laps after the stop are
excluded. After the stop the engine runs to the end of the race; it plans one
stop, not the stops after it, and Section~\ref{sec:committed} measures what that
costs the audit.

The audit replays real decisions; it does not forecast them. For every race
with a fitted model, the top \NFinishers{} classified finishers in Formula~1
(\NCars{} cars in endurance) who made at least one stop are replayed at their
\emph{first} stop. The model is asked \LookbackFone{} laps before that stop in
Formula~1 and \LookbackEnd{} in endurance, given the state as it was, and its
recommended lap is compared to the team's. Stops earlier than lap
\MinFirstStopFone{} (\MinFirstStopEnd{} in endurance) are excluded as incidents
rather than strategy. Rivals keep their real, historically observed plans: the
decision under study is one car's, the rest of the world is as it happened.

This is what makes the comparison possible and also what stops it being a
prediction claim. The decision point is defined relative to a stop that already
happened.

\subsection{The three baselines}

Scored on the same decisions, from the same artifacts, on absolute lap error
against the team's stop.

\textbf{B1, fixed interval.} Divide the race into equal stints:
$\ell^{\star} = \operatorname{round}\!\left(kL/(m+1)\right)$ for the $k$th of
$m$ stops. Uses no fitted quantity at all.

\textbf{B2, threshold.} Stop on the first lap at which the stint's accumulated
tyre loss exceeds the pit loss,
%
\begin{equation}
\beta\,\frac{a(a+1)}{2} \;>\; \pi,
\qquad\text{firing at}\qquad
a^{\star} = \frac{-1 + \sqrt{1 + 8\pi/\beta}}{2}.
\label{eq:threshold}
\end{equation}
%
Equation~\ref{eq:threshold} uses the fitted slope and the measured pit loss,
and nothing else --- no fuel
term, no neutralisation hazard, no distribution over outcomes. The gap between
B2 and the full engine is precisely what the Monte Carlo buys.

\textbf{B3, fuel deadline.} Run the tank out. Undefined in Formula~1, where
refuelling has been prohibited since 2010, and reported as undefined rather than
substituted with the race end.

Where a rule cannot fire --- B2 on a tyre that never accumulates enough loss
before the flag --- no lap is returned and that decision is not scored for that
rule. Coverage is reported alongside every error, because a rule answering a
fifth of the decisions and landing close on those has not beaten one that
answers all of them.

\section{Result 1: transfer is a property of the circuit-class}
\label{sec:transfer}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.86\textwidth]{r1_transfer.png}
\caption{Leave-one-race-out mean within-stint $R^2$, one point per
circuit-class. Of \NCircuitClasses{} measured, \NTransferAboveTwo{} clear
$\TransferThreshold{}$.}
\label{fig:transfer}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:transfer} shows the distribution. The maximum is
\BestTransfer{} at \BestTransferWhere{}; almost everywhere else a slope fitted
on past seasons predicts the next one no better than that season's own mean.

Grouping by car type, GT3 classes average \GTThreeMean{} (95\% CI \GTThreeCI{})
against \ProtoMean{} (\ProtoCI{}) for prototypes. The difference is
\TransferDiff{} with a 95\% cluster bootstrap interval of \TransferDiffCI{}, and
a permutation test on the group labels gives $p = \TransferP{}$. Both are
reported because they fail differently: the bootstrap assumes the clusters
resemble their population, the permutation assumes only exchangeability under
the null. Resampling is at the circuit-class, never the fold: folds inside a
circuit-class share a pooled fitted slope, and treating them as independent
would roughly quadruple the apparent sample.

The obvious explanation for instability is heterogeneous, performance-balanced
machinery. I can rule it out. ELMS LMP2 is a near-specification class --- one
chassis, one engine, no Balance of Performance --- and its slopes fail to
transfer exactly as the balanced GT3 fields do. Balance of Performance is
therefore not needed for the instability. That is narrower than saying the car
plays no part: the GT3--prototype difference above is a car-type effect, and it
is confounded with circuit, since the circuits where transfer works do not all
host every class. Where transfer does occur it tracks short circuits with cheap
stops, which is the same axis Result~2 turns on.

\subsection{What a stable slope could have scored}
\label{sec:ceiling}

A low score has two explanations that are indistinguishable from outside the
measurement. The slope moved between seasons, or there was never enough signal
in the laps for any slope to be recovered. Counting how few circuit-classes
clear a threshold cannot separate those, and the separation is the result.

So I measured the second one directly, on Formula~1, where the per-compound
fit and the lap data are richest. Lap times are rebuilt from each circuit's own
fit --- its driver--race intercepts, its fuel slope, and \emph{one} degradation
slope used for every season, so the slope is stable by construction --- plus
residuals resampled in whole stints, which keeps their within-stint correlation
rather than handing the model independent draws it would find easier to
predict. Running the real protocol on that gives the within-stint $R^2$ a
perfectly stable slope earns against the noise actually present.

The ceiling is far lower than the threshold, and it varies by an order of
magnitude between circuits: from \CeilingLowest{} at \CeilingLowestWhere{} to
\CeilingHighest{} at \CeilingHighestWhere{}. At
\NCeilingBelowThreshold{} of \NCeilingCircuits{} circuits a perfectly stable
slope could not have cleared $\TransferThreshold{}$. The threshold in
Figure~\ref{fig:transfer} is therefore reporting how much degradation signal a
circuit carries at least as much as it reports stability, and the
circuit-classes that clear it are partly the ones where the quantity is
measurable at all.

Taking the gap between ceiling and measured score instead --- the shortfall the
noise does not explain --- the picture is sharper than the count it replaces.
Of \NCeilingCircuits{} circuits, \NCeilingUnstable{} have slopes that genuinely
move, \NCeilingStable{} have slopes that are stable once the noise is priced
in, \NCeilingNoSignal{} carry no recoverable signal either way, and
\NCeilingBorderline{} sit between. Instability is real and it is the largest
group; it is not, as the raw scores imply, nearly universal.

\paragraph{The degree is chosen with the held-out season in view.} The folds
above select the polynomial degree by averaging cross-validated RMSE over every
fold, including the season then held out, which is a mild leak. Choosing the
degree inside each fold instead moves the mean score by \LeakageMean{} and at
most \LeakageMax{}. The leak is real and small. It is also not free to close:
at one circuit, per-fold selection takes the quadratic and extrapolates it off
a cliff, which is why the published protocol chooses once.
\NCeilingExcluded{} circuits are excluded from the counts above as degenerate
fits and named in the generated report.

\subsection{Two repairs a team would try first}
\label{sec:repairs}

If slopes move between seasons, two repairs suggest themselves, and both can be
tested on Formula~1 with the protocol unchanged.

\paragraph{Code the tyre by what it was.} The Formula~1 model carries one slope
per compound label, and the labels are relative. Pirelli nominates three
compounds of its range for each race, and the same circuit can receive a
different three from one season to the next, so last season's Medium may be
this season's Hard. I collected the nomination for all \NAllocationRaces{}
races from 2022 to 2025 from the race articles of Wikipedia, which cite Pirelli,
and checked it against Pirelli's own press releases, which state it in text for
\NAllocationPirelli{} of them and agree every time. When Pirelli added a compound
in 2023 it renamed its hardest one; a 2022 lap on that tyre is coded with the
name the same rubber carried afterwards, not with its old one. Recoding every
lap to the real compound and rerunning the leave-one-race-out protocol, both
codings scored on the same laps, changes nothing where the allocation stayed the
same. At the \NCompoundChanged{} of \NCompoundCircuits{} circuits where it
changed, the median score moves from \CompoundRelative{} to \CompoundReal{},
a median paired difference of \CompoundDiff{} \CompoundDiffCi{}. The real
compound scores better at \NCompoundBetter{} circuits and worse at
\NCompoundWorse{}, and its largest gain anywhere is \CompoundMaxGain{}. With
every circuit forced to the linear model, so that no quadratic can extrapolate
on a compound seen in one season, the difference is \CompoundLinearDiff{}
\CompoundLinearDiffCi{}. The recoding also has a cost the relative labels
hide: on average \CompoundUnseenPct{}\% of a held-out season's laps, and up to
\CompoundUnseenMaxPct{}\% at one circuit, are on a compound no other season of
that circuit used, and cannot be predicted at all. Relative labels are not what
breaks transfer.

\paragraph{Measure it on Friday.} A team need not rely on other seasons at all:
in second practice every car runs long runs on race fuel, on that weekend's
tyres and asphalt. A long run here is a practice stint long enough to fit a
slope to once its out-lap, in-lap and cool-down laps are dropped, and a
compound's Friday slope is used only when several cars ran one on it; on a
sprint weekend the only practice session is used, which is the case in
\NFridaySprint{} of the \NFridayRaces{} races. Inside a stint tyre age and fuel
burn advance together on Friday as on Sunday, so the Friday slope is the
quantity the race model predicts inside a stint and needs no fuel correction.
Scored on the same race laps, it does worse than other seasons: a median
within-stint $R^2$ of \FridayRaw{} against \FridayOther{}, lower in
\NFridayRawWorse{} of the \NFridayRaces{} races, with a median paired
difference of \FridayRawDiff{} \FridayRawDiffCi{} when whole circuits are
resampled. Part of that is a level difference: Friday long runs degrade faster
than the same compound does in the race, by a median of \FridayOffset{}\,s a
lap. Subtracting that gap, learned on every other circuit so that no race
informs its own correction, still leaves \FridayCorrected{}. Averaging the
corrected Friday shape with the other-seasons shape gives \FridayBoth{}, worse
than other seasons alone in \NFridayBothWorse{} of \NFridayRaces{} races
\FridayBothDiffCi{}. A Friday slope rests on a handful of runs per compound by
drivers managing fuel, engine modes and traffic in ways the race does not
repeat. A team reading its own Friday has information this protocol lacks, but
the timing data alone carry less about Sunday's degradation than other seasons
do. Neither repair moves Result~1.

\section{Result 2: the cost of the stop sets the strategy regime}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{r2_pit_loss_rule.png}
\caption{Left: class-level median pit loss against the share of race-seasons
where the tyre-optimal plan needs more stops than the fuel minimum. Right: every
race-season, with the empirical edge marked.}
\label{fig:pitloss}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:pitloss} plots the rule. An exact dynamic program plans each
endurance race under a hard fuel constraint
and reports whether the tyre-optimal plan requires more stops than the fuel
minimum. Across \NRaceSeasons{} race-seasons, \NTyreLimited{} are tyre-limited.

The class-level correlation between median pit loss and tyre-limited share is
$\PitLossR{}$ with a 95\% interval of \PitLossRCI{}, monotonic across all
classes with no inversion. That interval is bootstrapped over \emph{races},
recomputing each class summary inside every replicate; bootstrapping the class
summaries themselves would give an interval over six fixed championships, which
is not a source of variation that exists.

At race level, \NAboveEdge{} of \NRaceSeasons{} race-seasons have a pit loss
above \CheapStopEdge{}\,s and \NTyreLimitedAboveEdge{} of them is tyre-limited,
across every class.

\paragraph{Is this circular?} The optimiser decides the regime by comparing
what an extra stop costs against what the tyre gives back, so pit loss
predicting the regime is pit loss predicting one side of its own criterion. The
objection is fair and the answer has to be a measurement. If the stop cost were
doing all the work, the degradation slope would carry no information about the
regime once the stop cost is known. It carries some. Ranking the
\NRaceSeasons{} race-seasons by pit loss alone orders the \RegimeNTyreLimited{}
tyre-limited against the \RegimeNFuelLimited{} fuel-limited ones at an AUC of
\RegimeAucPitLoss{} (95\% CI \RegimeAucPitLossCI{}); by net degradation slope
alone, \RegimeAucSlope{} (\RegimeAucSlopeCI{}). Both are well clear of a coin
toss and the ordering between them is not close.

This does not establish that pit loss \emph{causes} the regime, and I do not
claim it: the two are related by construction. What it establishes is that the
comparison is asymmetric in practice. Knowing the cost of a stop tells you
nearly the whole answer across four championships; knowing how fast the tyre
wears tells you considerably less. The case that pit loss is exogenous to the
race outcome is made separately, from the fact that it varies far more between
circuits than between seasons of the same circuit.

\paragraph{Is the separation a class label, or the spread of one predictor?}
Two objections sit here and both have measurements rather than arguments.

The first is that pit loss simply varies more than the slope does, so an AUC
comparison flatters it. It cannot. The statistic above is the Mann--Whitney
form, computed from ranks, so it is invariant under any strictly increasing
transformation: standardising pit loss leaves it at
\RegimeAucStandardised{}, unmoved to three decimals. Rescaling is not available
as a correction because the objection does not reach a rank statistic.

The second is sharper. Pit loss is nearly constant inside a class, so its AUC
could be measuring class identity wearing a continuous disguise --- and the
class-level correlation above rests on one point per class. Ranking race-seasons
by their class's mean pit loss alone gives \RegimeAucClassLabel{}, well short of
\RegimeAucPitLoss{} for pit loss itself, so the label does not carry the result.
Nor is pit loss mostly a class property: \RegimeWithinClassShare{}\% of its
variance is \emph{within} class rather than between, which is what one would
expect of a quantity set by the geometry of a pit lane rather than by a car.
Recomputed inside each class, where class identity is held fixed by
construction, the cost of the stop still separates the two regimes in all
\NRegimeWithinClass{} classes where both regimes occur, between
\RegimeWithinClassMin{} and \RegimeWithinClassMax{}. The remaining
\NRegimeClassesOneRegime{} classes contain one regime only, so no AUC is
defined for them and none is reported.

The third objection is precision. Pit loss is measured from stop durations;
the slope is estimated, and a noisily measured predictor loses AUC even when
the quantity behind it matters as much. If that were the cause, the slope's
AUC should rise as the least precise slopes are dropped. It does not. Keeping
the \NPrecisionHalf{} race-seasons with the narrowest slope intervals gives
\PrecisionHalfSlopeAuc{} for the slope against \PrecisionHalfPitAuc{} for pit
loss, and keeping the most precise \NPrecisionThird{} gives
\PrecisionThirdSlopeAuc{} against \PrecisionThirdPitAuc{}, though with only
\NPrecisionThirdTyreLimited{} tyre-limited race-seasons left in that subset.
The gap is not an artefact of how well the slope is measured.

\paragraph{What the median pit loss is a median of.} It is taken over every
green-flag stop in the race-season, which in endurance racing includes stops
that change driver as well as stops that do not. A driver change is slower in
every class measured, so the class medians are not a measure of tyre-service
time alone. The class \emph{ordering} is unchanged whether the median is taken
over all stops, only those without a driver change, or only those with one,
which is what the correlation above depends on.

\paragraph{The condition behind it.} A linear slope $\beta$ over a stint of $n$
laps accumulates $\beta n(n+1)/2$ seconds of degradation, so an extra stop
repays its $\pi$ seconds when that sum exceeds $\pi$. I state it because it is
the readable form of the mechanism, and I do not use it: the dynamic program
above is exact under the fuel cap and the stop count is read from its solution.
The closed form is an approximation to that, checked against it rather than
substituted for it.

\paragraph{The rule is robust; the constant is not.} The edge sits at
\CheapStopEdge{}\,s because a single race puts it there; the next tyre-limited
race is at \EdgeWithoutDefining{}\,s, a drop of \EdgeDropPct{}\%. I do not
report a bootstrap interval for it, because the statistic is a maximum: it sits
on the boundary of its own support, so the bootstrap distribution is degenerate
above it and understates uncertainty below. Quote the rule; treat the number as
an order of magnitude.

\section{Inference}
\label{sec:inference}

Each interval above is a percentile bootstrap resampled at the level its data
varies at, and those levels differ: circuit-classes for the transfer
comparison, races for the pit-loss correlation. The choice is not cosmetic.
Resampling transfer folds instead of circuit-classes would treat
\NCircuitClasses{} clusters as roughly four times that many independent
observations, and the interval would narrow for no reason connected to the
data. Figure~\ref{fig:intervals} collects every result that carries one.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{s6_intervals.png}
\caption{Every result carrying a bootstrap interval. The two panels are
separate because a within-stint $R^2$ difference and a correlation are not
measured on the same scale, and a forest plot works by letting the reader
compare bar lengths. The cheap-stop edge is absent by design: it is a maximum, and a leave-one-out
sensitivity is reported for it instead of an interval it cannot support.}
\label{fig:intervals}
\end{figure}

The audit's central finding is a median over decisions that are not
independent: several drivers in one race share a track, a Safety Car and one
tyre allocation, so a bootstrap over decisions would understate its width in
the direction that flatters the result. The audit tables carry race
identifiers, so the race is the unit resampled.

That interval changes how Result~3 (Section~\ref{sec:audit}) should be read, and it is the reason this
section reports it per class rather than only for the pooled median. Of the
\NAuditScopes{} class-level medians, \NAuditContainsZero{} contain zero
(\AuditZeroClasses{}), and the gap in those two classes is not established.
Formula~1 is \AuditMedFone{} laps with a race-clustered interval of
\AuditCiFone{} over \AuditRacesFone{} races; IMSA GTD \AuditMedImsaGtd{}
\AuditCiImsaGtd{}; IMSA GTD PRO \AuditMedImsaGtdpro{} \AuditCiImsaGtdpro{};
IMSA GTP \AuditMedImsaGtp{} \AuditCiImsaGtp{}; WEC Hypercar
\AuditMedWecHypercar{} \AuditCiWecHypercar{}; ELMS LMP2 \AuditMedElmsLmptwo{}
\AuditCiElmsLmptwo{}; ELMS LMP2 Pro/Am \AuditMedElmsLmptwoProAm{}
\AuditCiElmsLmptwoProAm{}.

So the ladder reported in Result~3 is not a smooth gradient across the caution
rate. As the audit was first run, it is a large and resolved disagreement in
Formula~1 and in all three IMSA classes, against no established disagreement at all in WEC Hypercar and
ELMS LMP2. The ordering still tracks the caution rate, but the low end of it
is a statement about what I cannot resolve rather than about a small gap.
Section~\ref{sec:committed} then shows that the resolved part is mostly a
property of the audit rather than of the planner.

\section{Result 3: most of the planner--team gap was the question the audit asked}
\label{sec:audit}

The planner replayed here is the single-next-stop engine of
Section~\ref{sec:method}. It chooses the lap of the next stop to minimise one
car's expected race time against a linear degradation slope, a measured stop
cost and a neutralisation hazard, and it runs the stint after that stop to the
flag. It represents neither the tyre allocation, nor traffic, nor energy
management, nor a championship position worth protecting. Every sentence below
should be read as a disagreement between a model and a practice rather than as
evidence about which was faster.

The result first. With each team's own next stop held fixed, the planner
lands a median of \CommitAllAfter{} laps from the real stop in Formula~1
\CommitAllCi{}, and the interval contains zero in every endurance class. What
survives is \CommitOneAfter{} laps \CommitOneCi{} in one-stop races, where the
planner and the pit wall were always answering the same question
(Section~\ref{sec:committed}).

The route there is a methodological finding of its own, and the rest of this
section follows it. Run as a single-next-stop audit, which lets the planner
stretch its second stint to the flag, the same planner is \FoneMedian{} laps
late in Formula~1. Four explanations for that gap were tested and failed
before the fifth showed that the audit had been asking a different question
from the one the team answered. A comparison between an optimiser and practice
has to hold the team's committed strategy fixed, or it measures the difference
between the two questions.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{r3_audit_bias.png}
\caption{Model lap minus team lap, \NDecisions{} replayed first stops. Grey:
the audit as first run, with the planner's second stint run to the flag.
Colour: the same decisions replayed with the stint ending at the team's own
second stop (Section~\ref{sec:committed}). In Formula~1 a one-stop decision
keeps its first-run value; in endurance only decisions with a later stop can be
replayed, hence the smaller counts. Boxes show quartiles; the cloud behind each
is the sample.}
\label{fig:audit}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:audit} shows the whole distribution. Every real first stop
with a fitted model is replayed. The model is asked five
laps before the stop, given the state as it was, and its recommended lap
compared to the team's. This is a replay, not a forecast: the decision point is
defined relative to a stop that already happened, which is what makes the
comparison possible and also what stops it being a prediction claim.

In Formula~1 the optimiser stops later on \FoneLateShare{}\% of decisions, by a
median of \FoneLateMedian{} laps on those; over every decision, late or not, the
median is \FoneMedian{} laps. The endurance figures below are medians over every
decision, so \FoneMedian{} is the comparable one. In endurance the gap tracks the caution rate:
WEC \WecMedian{} laps at \WecCautionShare{}\% of first stops taken under
caution, ELMS \ElmsMedian{} at \ElmsCautionShare{}\%, IMSA \ImsaMedian{} at
\ImsaCautionShare{}\%.

Read that ladder with the race-clustered intervals in Section~\ref{sec:inference}
beside it. Its two lowest rungs, WEC Hypercar and ELMS LMP2, have intervals
containing zero: the ordering is real but the small gaps at the bottom of it
are not established, and only the Formula~1 and IMSA disagreements are --- as
first measured, before Section~\ref{sec:committed} removes most of them.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{s1_neutralisation_regimes.png}
\caption{How often each championship neutralises a race, split by kind. A
Safety Car bunches the field; a Full Course Yellow --- a Virtual Safety Car in
Formula~1 --- imposes a field-wide speed limit without bunching it, and the two
discount the cost of a stop by very different amounts. IMSA deployed no Safety
Car in any scoped race and neutralises almost every race by the other route, so
a figure showing only the first column would put IMSA at zero and contradict
its caution share above. The unit is the race, not the car: the flag is the
modal per-lap flag across the field, never one car's timing row. Classes are
not separated because every class in a race shares the same neutralisation.}
\label{fig:neutralisation}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:neutralisation} gives the neutralisation rates behind that
ladder. A stop taken under caution costs a fraction of a green-flag stop, so a
championship that neutralises often gives teams a reason to stop early that the
optimiser, which prices the stop at its green-flag cost, does not see. That
ordering is consistent with the gap, and it is not a test of it: three
championships is three points, and I do not fit a line through them.

\subsection{Testing the two candidate explanations}

I proposed two mechanisms and then attacked them.

\textbf{Absence of track position.} The engine optimises one car's expected race
time and cannot pay for an undercut, which is exactly why a team stops before it
has to. Re-running all \NDecisionsFone{} Formula~1 decisions through a
cover-aware Stackelberg engine consuming each circuit's measured overtaking
difficulty moves the recommendation \emph{away} from the real stop, not toward
it. \textbf{Rejected.}

Across the calendar the cover-aware recommendation lands a median of
\UndercutClosedMedian{} lap further from the real stop than the single-car one,
and only \UndercutShareImproving{}\% of decisions improve at all.

Two separate things follow and they should not be read together. The first is
about the hypothesis: modelling the cover does not move the recommendation
toward what teams did, so an unmodelled undercut does not account for the gap.
That holds under every rival-selection rule in Section~\ref{sec:rivalchoice},
including the one that fits the engine best. The second is about the test
rather than the hypothesis: part of the \emph{further} in that sentence was
an artefact of how the rival was chosen. Under the published selection the
cover-aware model is a median \RivalPositionClosed{} lap worse than the
single-car one, which reads as an engine that damages its own input; under the
standalone-time selection it is level at \RivalThravesClosed{} and improves
\RivalThravesBetter{} decisions against \RivalPositionBetter{}. The hypothesis
dies either way. It dies cleanly under the better selection, and the earlier
appearance of a model actively making things worse was in part a measurement
defect I have since fixed.

Two qualifications stand between the first of those and a clean refutation.

The first is that the covariate is thinner than its headline suggests.
Figure~\ref{fig:trackposition} shows a \TrackPositionRange{}-fold range across
\NCircuitsSwap{} circuits, which sounds decisive and is carried by its two
ends. \SwapLowestCircuit{} sits at \SwapLowest{} swaps per lap, a factor of
\SwapRunnerUpRatio{} below the next circuit, with a spread across its
\SwapLowestRaces{} races of only \SwapLowestSd{} --- the one entry that is
genuinely separated. The top of the range rests on \SwapHighestRaces{} races at
a circuit first run in 2023 and is the noisiest row in the table. In between,
the standard deviation across circuits (\SwapBetweenSd{}) is about the same as
the median standard deviation across races within a circuit
(\SwapWithinSd{}), so the twenty circuits in the middle are not separable from
one another on this measure.

The second is that the mechanism is not uniformly wrong. At
\SwapLowestCircuit{}, where overtaking is hardest and the covariate resolves
cleanly, the cover-aware engine does move toward the real stop, by a median of
\SwapLowestClosedMedian{} laps over \SwapLowestDecisions{} decisions, and the
rank correlation between swap rate and improvement is \UndercutSpearman{}
across the calendar. Both point the way the mechanism predicts. Neither is
remotely large enough: half a lap against a median discrepancy of
\FoneMedian{} laps is the right sign at the wrong order of magnitude.
Track position is doing something. It is not doing this.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.78\textwidth]{s4_track_position.png}
\caption{Adjacent-car swap rate per lap, by circuit. This is the primitive the
cover-aware engine consumes, shown so that the rejection above can be read
against the spread of the input, and not assumed to come from a flat one.}
\label{fig:trackposition}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Slopes biased toward durability.} A tyre that looks flatter than it is
makes staying out look cheaper. Measured against an independent source that
separates tyre wear from fuel burn by a different method on different data, the
median paired difference is negligible --- an error of that size moves a stop by
several race distances, not by ten laps. \textbf{Not detected.} I note that
comparing the two \emph{medians} instead of the median of paired differences
produces a small apparent bias that is an artefact of comparing summaries rather
than pairs.

\subsection{A third explanation, from published work}
\label{sec:thirdexplanation}

The two explanations tested above were mine. A third comes from
\citet{salminen2026}, who solves the two-car one-stop problem as a
perfect-information sequential game and derives the earliest lap on which an
undercut cannot be answered. It is the only mechanism I have found that
predicts stopping \emph{before} the time-optimal lap, which is the direction of
the disagreement reported here: a chaser stops when the leader's answer expires,
and waiting for the time optimum hands the leader a window.

The leader has two answers in that model. The overcut needs a tyre advantage of
$(o + \varepsilon)/\theta$ laps, where $o$ is an overtaking threshold in
seconds. I hold no such quantity --- what this project measures per circuit is
an adjacent-pair swap probability per lap, a different object that does not
convert into one --- so I implement only the position-keeping defence, which is
efficient while $\theta l_u + \varepsilon < g$ and therefore expires at a tyre
age of $(g - \varepsilon)/\theta$. Where the overcut is unavailable, the
earliest undefendable undercut is the lap after that. I set $\varepsilon = 0$
throughout: estimating it would mean reading a chaser's pace while it sits in
dirty air, which inflates it, and a larger $\varepsilon$ expires the defence
earlier and so moves the prediction toward the real stop.

\paragraph{It fails, and by how much.} Across the \DOnePredicted{} decisions
carrying a prediction, the earliest undefendable undercut lands a median of
\DOneMedianError{} laps from the real stop, against \DOneBaselineError{} for the
single-car optimiser on the same decisions. It is closer on \DOneCloser{} and
further on \DOneFurther{}. Fed with the gaps and slopes measured here, the
condition says a Formula~1 leader can defend an undercut for longer than the
race lasts, so a chaser should never undercut at all.

The failure has a number rather than a story behind it. Setting $l_u$ to the
tyre age of the stop a team actually made gives the degradation rate at which
the defence would have expired exactly then,
$\theta^{*} = (g - \varepsilon)/l_u$. Its median is
\DOneImpliedTheta{}\,s/lap against a measured \DOneMeasuredTheta{}, a ratio of
\DOneThetaRatio{} with quartiles \DOneThetaRatioIQR{}, and $\theta^{*}$ exceeds
the measured rate on \DOnePctThetaAbove{}\% of decisions. A rate of
\DOneImpliedTheta{}\,s/lap sits at the \DOneThetaPercentile{}th percentile of
every slope fitted in this work. The gap is therefore not a matter of
calibration: for the equilibrium to reproduce what teams do, tyres would have to
degrade at a rate this data almost never shows.

\paragraph{A reading I have not established.} $\theta l_u$ prices the
defender's loss over a single lap on a tyre $l_u$ laps old. At a measured
\DOneMeasuredTheta{}\,s/lap and a tyre the age teams stop at, that is under a
second, which the median \DOneMedianGap{}\,s lead covers easily. What wins a
real undercut is the advantage of a tyre on its first flying lap over one at the
end of its life, and a linear slope has no term for that. Measuring it directly
is a different estimator and I have not attempted it.

\paragraph{What holds whatever the verdict.} Of the
\DOneDecisions{} decisions, \DOneNoRival{} belong to a car with nobody ahead of
it on the clock within one lap. The race leader has no undercut to perform, so
roughly a quarter of the audited set carries no prediction under any two-car
model, which bounds what this family of explanations could ever account for. For
the remaining \DOneChasers{}, the gap to the leader is a median
\DOneMedianGap{}\,s, and on \DOneWithinPitLoss{} of \DOneReachable{} it is
smaller than the circuit's measured pit loss. Whether the position is reachable
by stopping first is therefore not the binding constraint, which is the opposite
of what I expected to find.

\paragraph{Defects found while building this.} All three inflated the
defence's window, so all three made this negative result look stronger than it
is, and I report them for that reason. Comparing cumulative race time with no
bound found rivals a full lap away; the nearest car ahead is now capped at one
green lap and the widest retained gap is \DOneMaxGap{}\,s. The expiry is a tyre
age and was being compared against a lap number, which agree on only
\DOnePctAgeIsLap{}\% of these decisions. And the breadth layer's pit-loss table
names circuits differently from the lap files, which still drops
\DOneStaleDropped{} of \DOneChasers{} values if joined on the slug. Each now has
a test.

\subsection{A fourth explanation, and the sign it comes back with}
\label{sec:freshtyre}

The most natural candidate explanation is structural rather than
empirical. A linear slope has no one-off gain at a stop, so an optimiser built
on it should always recommend stopping later than a pit wall buying an immediate
jump in pace, and pricing that jump in should close the gap.

The shape a fit misses is visible in its own residuals, so the claim needs no
new machinery. A fit forces its residuals to average zero overall; what carries
the answer is the profile against tyre age, where negative means laps faster
than the model says. Pooled over \NFreshCircuits{} Formula~1 circuits, the
youngest measured age carries \FreshResid{}\,s and the next \FreshResidNext{}\,s
--- laps on a new set come in \emph{slower} than the fit expects, and the sign
only turns over once the set is several laps old. Per circuit, fresh laps are
faster than modelled at \NFreshFaster{} of \NFreshCircuits{}, median
\FreshMedianBonus{}\,s. The out-lap is already outside the modelling frame, so
this is the first flying laps on the new set, which is what a stop buys.

That is tyre warm-up, and it is the opposite of the effect the objection
predicts. The engine prices a stop as an instant return to the slope's
intercept, so it is already \emph{over}stating what a stop is worth; correcting
it would push the recommended lap later still and widen the disagreement rather
than close it. Four candidate explanations have now been tested here and all
four have failed, three of them in the direction that makes the gap larger.

\subsection{A fifth explanation: the question the audit asked}
\label{sec:committed}

The four explanations above all look for something the planner misprices. The
fifth is in the audit. The engine plans one stop and runs the stint after it to
the flag, so for a car that stopped once it was answering the question the pit
wall answered. For a car that stopped again, it was not: the team's second stint
ended at its second stop, and an engine made to stretch one set of tyres to the
end will place the first stop later for that reason alone.

The published gap splits accordingly. Over the \NCommitOne{} Formula~1 decisions
by drivers who stopped once, the median is \CommitOneBefore{} laps
\CommitOneBeforeCi{}; over the \NCommitMulti{} by drivers who stopped again it
is \CommitMultiBefore{} \CommitMultiBeforeCi{}, and \CommitThreeBefore{} for
three or more stops. Inside the \NCommitWithinRaces{} races containing both
kinds of decision the multi-stop median exceeds the one-stop median by
\CommitWithinGap{} laps, so the split is not only a difference between circuits.

I then replayed every decision whose driver stopped again with the race
ending, for the engine, at that driver's real second stop. Everything after that
stop runs on fresh tyres whichever first-stop lap is chosen, so it is common to
every candidate and drops out: the optimum over the shortened horizon is exactly
the optimum given the team's own second stop. Nothing else changes; replayed
with the full horizon, the same code reproduces every published recommendation
in a random sample of forty. Leaving out the \NCommitDropped{} decisions whose
real stop falls outside the shortened window, and with the team's strategy held
fixed, the Formula~1 median falls from \CommitAllBefore{} to \CommitAllAfter{} laps \CommitAllCi{},
and among multi-stop decisions from \CommitMultiBefore{} to \CommitMultiAfter{}
\CommitMultiCi{}. In endurance the same replay, with each stint also bounded by
the fuel range, covers \NEndCommit{} decisions, and the interval contains zero
in all \NEndCommitContainsZero{} classes. The first-run medians below are over
those replayable decisions only, so they differ slightly from the
whole-class medians in Figure~\ref{fig:audit}: IMSA GTD falls from
\EndCommitImsaGtdBefore{} to \EndCommitImsaGtdAfter{} \EndCommitImsaGtdCi{},
IMSA GTD PRO from \EndCommitImsaGtdproBefore{} to \EndCommitImsaGtdproAfter{}
\EndCommitImsaGtdproCi{}, and IMSA GTP from \EndCommitImsaGtpBefore{} to
\EndCommitImsaGtpAfter{} \EndCommitImsaGtpCi{}.

Two objections have to be met before that is read as agreement. The first is
hindsight: a second stop taken under a Safety Car was not planned at the
decision lap. Keeping only the \NCommitGreen{} decisions whose second stop was
under green leaves the Formula~1 median at \CommitGreenAfter{}
\CommitGreenCi{}. The second is that fixing the second stop shrinks the set of
laps the engine can pick from, and a narrow enough window makes agreement
automatic. In Formula~1 it does not: the window is a median of
\CommitWindow{} laps, inside which a lap drawn uniformly would miss the real
stop by a median of \CommitUniformMiss{} and the window's midpoint by
\CommitMidpointMiss{}, against \CommitEngineMiss{} for the engine. In
endurance the engine beats both chance baselines in only
\NEndCommitInformative{} of \NEndCommitClasses{} classes, the three IMSA ones
(GTD: window \EndCommitImsaGtdWindow{}, engine \EndCommitImsaGtdMiss{},
uniform \EndCommitImsaGtdUniform{}, midpoint \EndCommitImsaGtdMidpoint{}). In
WEC Hypercar and both ELMS classes the fuel range leaves a window of
\EndCommitWecHypercarWindow{} to \EndCommitElmsLmptwoProAmWindow{} laps, the
engine does no better than chance, and the replay is uninformative there ---
which is consistent with those being the classes where the published gap was
never established.

What survives is the one-stop residual. Where the engine and the team were
answering the same question, the engine still stops \CommitOneAfter{} laps
later \CommitOneCi{}. That is the part of Result~3 the audit design does not
explain.

\subsection{What the remaining gap costs}
\label{sec:deviationcost}

A gap in laps is not a gap in time, and the planner's own price for it is a
model output. The committed replay gives both: for each first stop, the
planner's lap with the team's next stop fixed, and the median time the planner
predicts the team's lap cost against its own. Over the same stretch of the real
race, from the decision lap to the team's next stop or to the flag, I measured
each car's elapsed time against what its own median green-flag lap predicts for
that many laps, and compared cars within a race, which share the track, the
weather and the tyre allocation. A race fixed effect absorbs what is common to
the field, the window's length is a control, and a window containing a Safety
Car, a Virtual Safety Car or a red flag for that car is dropped, since a stop
under neutralisation is cheaper by an amount the planner's cost does not
describe.

That leaves \NDeviationCars{} first stops in \NDeviationRaces{} races. They sit
a median of \DeviationMedianLaps{} laps from the planner's lap, a distance the
planner prices at a median of \DeviationPredicted{}\,s. In the races, each lap
of distance from the planner's lap goes with \DeviationPerLap{}\,s of extra
elapsed time \DeviationPerLapCi{}, against \DeviationPlannerPerLap{}\,s by the
planner's own pricing. Regressed on the planner's predicted cost directly, the
slope is \DeviationSlope{} \DeviationSlopeCi{}, where one would mean the
model's costs show up in the clock unchanged. Both intervals contain zero, and
both contain the planner's price. The races cannot tell them apart because the
quantity is small: between cars of the same race the excess time has a median
standard deviation of \DeviationSpread{}\,s, an order of magnitude more than the
planner says the typical gap costs.

This is association, not an experiment. Teams leave the planner's lap for
reasons it cannot see --- traffic, a rival's stop, a car problem --- and those
reasons have costs of their own, in either direction. What it does establish is
the scale. The residual Result~3 leaves is worth tenths of a second per lap of
distance, inside the flat part of the optimum where a single race cannot
distinguish the team's lap from the planner's.

\subsection{Comparison against three baselines}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{s5_baselines.png}
\caption{Median absolute lap error against the real stop, one row per
class rather than per championship. IMSA's three classes run the same rounds
under pit losses of \ImsaGtpPitLoss{}, \ImsaGtdPitLoss{} and
\ImsaGtdproPitLoss{} seconds, so B3 --- run the tank out --- means a different
thing in each and one IMSA row would describe none of them.}
\label{fig:baselines}
\end{figure}

Three rules were scored on \NScored{} of the same decisions, from the same
artifacts, on the same metric (Figure~\ref{fig:baselines} and
Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). B1 divides the race
into equal stints and uses no fitted quantity at all. B2 stops once the tyre's
accumulated loss exceeds the pit loss, using the fitted slope and the measured
pit loss and nothing else. B3 runs the fuel load out, and is undefined in
Formula~1, where refuelling has been prohibited since 2010 --- I report it as
undefined rather than substituting the race end.

Results are reported per class rather than per championship. IMSA runs GTP, GTD
and GTD PRO at the same rounds with median pit losses of \ImsaGtpPitLoss{}, \ImsaGtdPitLoss{} and \ImsaGtdproPitLoss{} seconds,
so a single IMSA row averages three strategy regimes into a number describing
none of them. That grouping also concealed a difference worth seeing: GTP, the
IMSA class with the dearest stops, has the smallest disagreement of the three.
