A rule of thumb sits closer to practice than the exact optimiser in
\NClassesRuleWins{} of \NClassesScored{} classes, ties it in
\NClassesRuleTies{} and loses in \NClassesOptimiserWins{}. In
\NClassesBoneWins{} of those classes the winning rule is B1, which uses no
fitted quantity whatsoever --- only the race length and the number of stops
the tank forces. In the two it does not win, it ties the optimiser rather
than losing to it.

That comparison is against the audit as first run. Held to each team's next
stop, the optimiser is closer than every rule in \NClassesCommitBeatsRules{}
classes and ties the best rule in \NClassesCommitTiesRules{}, the last column
of Table~\ref{tab:baselines}. It is not a like-for-like contest: the replay
knows the team's second stop and the rules do not, and in WEC Hypercar and
ELMS the replay was shown above to be uninformative. What it does show is that
the rules' advantage over the first-run optimiser came from the question that
optimiser was asked, not from information it lacked.

\emph{Closer to what teams did} is not \emph{better}: every number here scores
agreement with practice, never which plan was faster.

\section{Result 4: which car counts as the rival is under-determined}
\label{sec:rivalchoice}

The replay above pairs each
audited car with its nearest neighbour on classified position, which Thraves
objected chooses the car ahead on some decisions and the car behind on others
while the decision order is fixed, and which leaves
\NTiedDecisions{} of \NDecisionsFone{} decisions as ties between an equidistant
neighbour in front and one behind. He proposed a criterion in its place:
estimate for each car the total race time it would set under its own optimal
strategy in the absence of competition, and take as rival the car whose
estimated time is closest.

I implement it with the same exact dynamic program the audit already uses,
scoring each car from its own median green lap, the circuit-compound
degradation posterior for the tyre it is running, and the circuit's measured
pit loss. The compound term matters for the reason he gave: two cars at
identical raw pace reach their optima on different laps if one is on a
faster-wearing tyre. Formula~1 has not refuelled since 2010, so the fuel cap is
the race distance and never binds, and what the program trades off is
degradation against stop cost. The median gap in estimated standalone race time
between an audited car and the rival this picks is \RivalStandaloneGap{}\,s
over a full race.

Table~\ref{tab:rivalrules} runs \NRivalRules{} rules against the same decisions.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Rival-selection rules on the same Formula~1 decisions. Errors are
signed in laps, positive meaning later than the team stopped. \emph{Closed} is
the single-car absolute error minus the cover-aware one, so a positive value
would mean modelling the rival moved the recommendation toward the team's
choice. The position-ahead rule scores fewer decisions because a race leader
has no car ahead of it.}
\label{tab:rivalrules}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrr}
\toprule
rule & scored & cover-aware & closed (median) & closed (mean) & improved \\
\midrule
nearest on position & \RivalPositionScored{} & \RivalPositionAdv{} & \RivalPositionClosed{} & \RivalPositionMeanClosed{} & \RivalPositionBetter{} \\
within one pit loss & \RivalPiWindowScored{} & \RivalPiWindowAdv{} & \RivalPiWindowClosed{} & \RivalPiWindowMeanClosed{} & \RivalPiWindowBetter{} \\
car ahead on the clock & \RivalDOneScored{} & \RivalDOneAdv{} & \RivalDOneClosed{} & \RivalDOneMeanClosed{} & \RivalDOneBetter{} \\
nearest standalone time & \RivalThravesScored{} & \RivalThravesAdv{} & \RivalThravesClosed{} & \RivalThravesMeanClosed{} & \RivalThravesBetter{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Two things come out of it and they point opposite ways.

The choice of rival is consequential. His rule and the published one name the
same car on \PctRivalThravesAgrees{}\% of decisions, and all
\NRivalRules{} rules agree on \NRivalAllAgree{} of the \NRivalAllApply{}
decisions where all of them apply. Four defensible readings of the word
``rival'' disagree about which car to model four times out of five.

It does not move Result~3. The cover-aware recommendation stays later than the
real stop under every rule, by a median of \RivalThravesAdv{} laps at best
against \FoneLateMedian{} for the single-car model it is meant to improve on.
What his rule does change is the penalty: under the published selection the
cover-aware model sits a median \RivalPositionClosed{} lap further from the
real stop than the single-car one, and under his it is level at
\RivalThravesClosed{}, improving \RivalThravesBetter{} decisions against
\RivalPositionBetter{}. The defect he identified is therefore real, and
correcting it does not produce the agreement the adversarial model was built
to find.

He also named the limit of his own proposal, and I state it as he put it: at
the extreme the choice of rival becomes endogenous, since each car's strategy
depends on the others. The standalone time this heuristic sorts on is computed
with no competition in it, which is what makes it computable and equally what
makes it an approximation. I do not resolve this. A selection rule that
accounted for the interaction would have to solve the joint problem the
selection is a step toward, and nothing here does that.

A second approximation is mine rather than his. The standalone time is the
whole race from the start rather than the remaining race from the decision lap,
so it pairs cars by capability instead of by where they have got to. His
formulation is the former and it is what I implement; the latter would answer
a different question.

\paragraph{What this does and does not claim.} How far four rules disagree
depends on how different they are, and four near-restatements of one criterion
would of course agree. The obvious objection is therefore that the rules were
chosen to diverge. They were not, and the provenance of two of them is what
answers it.

The car-ahead rule is not a reading I selected. It is the pairing
\citet{salminen2026} defines his defences on: his leader and chaser are
whichever two cars are adjacent on the clock, so testing his model at all
forces that rule and no other. The standalone-time rule was proposed to me by
Charles Thraves, in correspondence, as a criterion he thought the audit should
use instead of mine; he is an author of the Stackelberg treatment
(\citealp{aguad2024}; \citealp{carrasco2022}) whose framing this project's
adversarial component reuses. Neither rule was constructed here, neither was
constructed against the other, and neither was introduced because it
disagreed --- the disagreement is what came back.

The disagreement is also bounded. No decision produces four distinct cars, and
\NRivalTwoCars{} of \NRivalAllApply{} produce exactly two. The claim is that a
rival is not determined by the timing data together with a defensible
criterion, which is weaker than saying it is undefined and strong enough to
matter for any model that assumes one.

The game-theoretic branch of this literature is built on a two-car abstraction.
\citet{aguad2024} solve a Stackelberg game between two drivers,
\citet{devries2026} pose a two-agent problem per lap, and
\citet{salminen2026} derives his equilibrium for a leader and a chaser. Each is
internally consistent and none of them has occasion to say which two cars those
are in a real race, because the question does not arise inside the abstraction.
Measured against real decisions, the identification is the part that gives way.

\section{Threats to validity}
\label{sec:threats}

\paragraph{Estimators built here and withdrawn.} A piecewise race-time basis intended to
absorb track evolution was validated on synthetic races and then withdrawn twice
on real ones: real fields sit close to the degenerate boundary where tyre age
and race time share most of their variance after fixed effects. Formula~1's
median identifiability is \NIdentifiability{}, well outside the range the basis
was shown to work in. I report the omitted variable as diagnosed and unfixed
rather than applying a correction that fails silently.

\paragraph{Result~1 bounds reuse, not refitting.} Giona Fieni (ETH
Z\"urich) stated the scope limit on this result more sharply than I had. A
primarily model-based policy treats fitted degradation curves as placeholders
and retunes them for each car and circuit, so it never depends on a slope
transferring to a season it has not seen. Result~1 measures the stability of
reused data-driven parameters. That bounds approaches which carry fitted
parameters forward, and says nothing against a design that refits as a matter
of course; on that design's own terms it is an argument for refitting.

The concession stops there. If measured behaviour were stable once the physics
is fixed, the near-specification control field should have been the one that
transferred: one chassis, one engine, no Balance of Performance, a single tyre
supplier. It fails as the performance-balanced fields do. So either lap time
carries large effects that are not the tyre, or the retuning step is doing more
than retuning. I read it as the first, and the track evolution withdrawn above
is my candidate for part of what it is.

\paragraph{The audit was not a fair comparison, and most of Result~3 was
that.} The engine plans one stop and runs to the flag; a pit wall chooses a lap
inside a strategy it has already committed to. Section~\ref{sec:committed}
holds the team's next stop fixed and most of the gap disappears. Three limits
remain. Holding the second stop fixed gives the engine the team's plan in
hindsight; restricting to green-flag second stops answers the part of that
objection that concerns opportunistic stops, not the part that concerns a plan
revised during the race. The engine still represents neither the tyre
allocation nor traffic, so the one-stop residual of \CommitOneAfter{} laps may
yet be either. And in WEC Hypercar and ELMS the replay cannot discriminate,
because the fuel range leaves the engine too few laps to choose from.
Section~\ref{sec:deviationcost} prices the residual from the races
themselves, and the price is small; pricing it does not explain it, and that
measurement is an association between cars, open to every reason a team had
for its lap.

\paragraph{Drivers manage tyres to the stint they were given.} A driver told
to make a set last a long stint drives it more gently, so the slope a fit
measures depends partly on the strategy the team chose. A planner fitted on
those slopes will tend to find long stints affordable, which pushes in the
direction of the one-stop residual, and season-to-season changes in how teams
manage tyres would show up as the instability of Result~1. The cross-source
check in Section~\ref{sec:audit} separates tyre wear from fuel burn, not this.
Public timing cannot remove it; it could be bounded by comparing stints of the
same car with different planned lengths, which I have not done.

\paragraph{Unresolved slopes, carried forward anyway.} Of the
\NCoefficientsFone{} Formula~1 degradation coefficients,
\NCoefCrossingZero{} have a cluster-robust interval containing zero, and
\PctCompoundOverlap{}\% of compound pairs within a circuit have intervals that
overlap each other. Every one of them is carried forward regardless. Screening
on the resolved ones would select on the dependent variable --- circuit-classes
with tight slopes are exactly the ones likeliest to transfer --- and the
transfer result would then be partly an artefact of the screen. The cost is
that the weak transfer reported in Section~\ref{sec:transfer} is a mixture of
genuine instability and of parameters the data never pinned down.
Section~\ref{sec:ceiling} separates those two for Formula~1 by measuring what a
stable slope could have scored against the same noise, and the mixture turns
out to matter: most circuits cannot clear the quoted threshold even with a
slope that does not move. The endurance classes are not separated this way,
and their counts should be read with that in mind.

\paragraph{Constants resting on very little.} The cheap-stop edge of
\CheapStopEdge{}\,s is a maximum set by one race; drop it and the edge falls to
\EdgeWithoutDefining{}\,s, \EdgeDropPct{}\%. The second-best transfer score,
\ThinTransfer{} at \ThinTransferWhere{}, is a mean over \ThinTransferFolds{}
folds running from \ThinTransferLow{} to \ThinTransferHigh{} --- a spread of
\ThinTransferSpread{}, wider than most circuit-classes' entire score, and it
should not be read beside \BestTransferWhere{}'s \BestTransfer{}, which
averages \BestTransferFolds{} folds spanning \BestTransferSpread{}. Same
circuit, same protocol, an order of magnitude more stable. The instability is
therefore not a property of the circuit alone. And the top of
the track-position range rests on \SwapHighestRaces{} races at a circuit first
run in 2023. The rules these support are not thin --- \NAboveEdge{}
race-seasons sit above the edge with \NTyreLimitedAboveEdge{} tyre-limited
among them --- but the constants are, and they are quoted here as orders of
magnitude. A full accounting is generated into
\texttt{reports/cross\_series/thin\_evidence.md}.

\paragraph{Compound is unavailable in endurance.} The endurance degradation
models are net-slope models. Comparisons between the Formula~1 per-compound
coefficients and endurance net slopes are made only where the quantity is
genuinely comparable.

\paragraph{Neutralisation regimes are not poolable.} IMSA records no Safety Car
in any scoped race and a Full Course Yellow in nearly all of them; WEC and ELMS
are Safety-Car championships at very different rates. Any pooled endurance
neutralisation model would sit between these and describe none of them, so they
are never merged.

\paragraph{Some layers cannot be rebuilt from a clone.} The
breadth-degradation and reliability layers read a third-party export that is not
redistributed here. Their outputs are committed, so every downstream consumer
and every test runs offline; what is blocked is rebuilding them from source.
Section~\ref{sec:reproducibility} names them, and names the one whose blockage
reaches a published result.

\section{Reproducibility}
\label{sec:reproducibility}

Every artifact derived from committed data is regenerated by continuous
integration, which fails on any difference between the working tree and the
repository, including files a generator wrote and nobody committed.

The state these results were computed from is archived on Zenodo and,
through it, in Software Heritage and OpenAIRE. The concept identifier
\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22726130}
resolves to the newest version of the deposit. The release archived alongside
this paper carries its own frozen identifier, recorded in the repository's
\texttt{CITATION.cff}, for anyone who needs the exact state a figure came from
rather than the current one.

\paragraph{The blocked layers, named.} \NBlockedLayers{} layers read
third-party exports this repository does not redistribute, so those layers
cannot be regenerated from a clone: the Formula~1 breadth layer and the
Formula~1 and WEC reliability tables. Their outputs are committed, so
everything downstream of them runs offline, and the rest of the project ---
Formula~1 core, WEC, IMSA, ELMS, the simulator, the audits and every
cross-series layer --- reproduces from a clone with no external download. The
Pirelli nominations and the practice laps of Section~\ref{sec:repairs} are
committed with the scripts that collected them, so they too are read offline.

One of the three is load-bearing. The cross-source slope check that rejected
one of the candidate explanations for the gap in Result~3 rests on the breadth
layer, whose input a reader cannot obtain from this repository. Reproducing that
rejection requires the external source, which is named in the repository along
with what each blocked layer reads and writes.

Every number in this manuscript is a macro generated by
\texttt{scripts/make\_paper\_numbers.py} from the committed artifacts; the
source of this paper contains no digits. A separate test recomputes each
published headline from its artifact and asserts the formatted result appears in
the document that publishes it, which is stricter than recomputing alone.

\section{Conclusion}

What this paper offers is a protocol and what came back from it. Degradation
slopes rarely transfer, and where they do it is a property of the
circuit-class rather than of the championship; Balance of Performance is not
needed for the instability, and the effect of car type cannot be separated
here from the circuits each type races on. Whether an extra
stop can ever pay is decided by the cost of the stop, which separates the two
regimes at an AUC of \RegimeAucPitLoss{} against \RegimeAucSlope{} for the
tyre. And a time-optimal planner appeared to disagree with professional
practice by a median of \FoneMedian{} laps in Formula~1. I proposed two
explanations, tested both and lost both; I took a third from published work,
which has the right sign and fails on the quantity it depends on by a factor of
\DOneThetaRatio{}; a fourth comes back with the wrong sign
(Section~\ref{sec:freshtyre}). The fifth was the audit: asked to plan the
stint the team would actually run, the planner lands \CommitAllAfter{} laps
from the real stop rather than \CommitAllBefore{}, and no endurance class keeps
an established gap (Section~\ref{sec:committed}). Simpler rules landed closer
to practice than the first-run audit in \NClassesRuleWins{} of
\NClassesScored{} classes. Two repairs a team would reach for first, coding the
tyre by its real compound and measuring degradation on Friday, both leave
transfer where it was or worse (Section~\ref{sec:repairs}).

And the rival that a competition-aware model should answer is
under-determined: \NRivalRules{} defensible rules name the same car on
\NRivalAllAgree{} of \NRivalAllApply{} decisions, which constrains every model
built on a two-car abstraction.

What remains of the planner--team gap is \CommitOneAfter{} laps in one-stop
races, where the planner and the team were answering the same question. In
the races it is worth tenths of a second per lap of distance, within the noise
between cars of the same race (Section~\ref{sec:deviationcost}). It is smaller
than the gap this paper set out to explain, and it is the one I would most like
someone else to explain.

\section*{Data and code availability}

Every quantity in this paper is derived from committed artifacts by
scripts in a public repository, which also contains the data, the
figures and the tests:
\url{https://github.com/mohammedmedjadj/Motorsport-Strategy-Lab}. The
state the results were computed from is archived and citable at
\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22726130}.

\section*{Acknowledgements}

Several researchers replied to cold emails about this work. Three of those
replies changed what the repository contains, and what they changed is set out
here rather than thanked in general terms.

Charles Thraves (Universidad de Chile) identified the rival-selection defect in
the adversarial replay: minimising absolute classified-position distance picks
the car ahead on some decisions and the car behind on others, and with
equidistant neighbours the choice is incidental. He then proposed the
standalone-optimal-time heuristic tested in
Section~\ref{sec:rivalchoice}, confirmed that
compound and tyre-age differences in lap time are enough to move the relative
timing, and named the endogeneity that bounds his own proposal.

Wytze de Vries (TU Eindhoven) raised two measurement objections to Result~2:
that a class-level median pit loss pools two-tyre stops with full service
including a driver change, and that part of the correlation may run backwards,
since tyre-limited races carry less fuel and so stop faster. Both were tested;
the first holds and does not disturb the class ordering, and the second has the
sign he predicted at a magnitude too small to account for the result.

Jorn van Kampen (TU Eindhoven) described the same structure from electric
endurance racing, where the charging stop is long enough that a tyre change is
treated as negligible and is not optimised separately.

Giona Fieni (ETH Z\"urich) drew the line between a result about reused
data-driven parameters and a result about model-based policy, which is the
scope limit now stated in Section~\ref{sec:threats}; and held that once the
physics is known the behaviour follows, which is the position the
near-specification control field is set against there.

None of them is responsible for what this manuscript says.
